introduction-the-multiplication-problem.core: Series count is the product of each label's distinct values: 50 routes × 5 status codes × 4 methods × 200 pods is already 200,000 series for one metric, and histogram buckets multiply it again by ~12. Add one unbounded label (user_id, request path, session) and it becomes millions. Memory, query latency and SaaS bills scale with series, so one change can take down monitoring or blow the budget.

first_principles.problem: A deploy adds a 'path' label with raw URLs, and active series jump from 2 million to 40 million overnight.
truths: Pod churn creates new series constantly.
derivation: Account for **pod churn** (new series per pod).

analogy.title: A menu with every combination listed
analogy.story: Listing every combination of 50 dishes, 5 sizes and 200 table numbers produces an absurdly long menu.
analogy.breaks: Menus are printed once; series are created continuously with churn.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows why one label can destroy a TSDB.

check.q: Why do histograms amplify cardinality problems?
check.a: Each bucket is a separate series, so every label combination is multiplied by the number of buckets.

detecting-the-culprit.core: Find cardinality culprits with TSDB status (Prometheus /tsdb-status lists top metrics, labels and label-value pairs by series count), queries like topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"})), per-label counts on a suspicious metric, ingestion-rate and head-series growth graphs correlated with deploys, and vendor usage dashboards. Then trace the metric to its owning service and code.

first_principles.problem: Prometheus memory doubles and nobody knows which of 3,000 metrics is responsible.
derivation: Count **series per label** on the suspect.

analogy.title: Finding which room is flooding
analogy.story: Check the water meter per room instead of searching the whole house.
analogy.breaks: Floods are visible; series growth is only seen in stats.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Culprit: raw path label on latency histogram.

code.text:
curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/status/tsdb | jq '.data.seriesCountByMetricName[:5]'
# [{"name":"http_request_duration_seconds_bucket","value":18400000}, ...]
# then:
# count by (path) (http_request_duration_seconds_count)   → 1.5M distinct paths

check.q: Which Prometheus endpoint lists the metrics with the most series?
check.a: /api/v1/status/tsdb (TSDB status), including seriesCountByMetricName and label statistics.

mitigation-strategy-1-remove-the-label.core: The quickest fix is to stop producing the bad label. In code, replace raw values with bounded ones (route template instead of path, status class instead of code, bucketed tenant tier instead of tenant ID). In the scrape, use metric_relabel_configs with labeldrop or a replace to normalise values before ingestion. Move per-entity detail to logs or traces, where high cardinality is cheap.

first_principles.problem: A metric's user_id label must be removed immediately to stop Prometheus from OOM-crashing.
truths: Labels can be dropped at scrape time.

analogy.title: Removing a column from a spreadsheet
analogy.story: If 'customer name' creates a million rows, drop it from the summary sheet and keep it in the detailed records.
analogy.breaks: Spreadsheets recalc instantly; existing series remain until retention expires.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Series count drops immediately for new samples.

code.text:
metric_relabel_configs:
  - action: labeldrop
    regex: user_id
  - source_labels: [path]
    regex: '/api/orders/[0-9]+'
    target_label: path
    replacement: '/api/orders/:id'

check.q: Why put user IDs in trace attributes rather than metric labels?
check.a: Traces and logs store per-event data cheaply, while each metric label value creates a new long-lived series.

mitigation-strategy-2-aggregate-before-s.core: Sometimes the dimension is useful for computation but not for storage. Aggregate before storage: Prometheus recording rules pre-compute sum by (service, route) so dashboards query cheap series, and pipeline aggregation (Grafana Adaptive Metrics, Mimir or Thanos aggregation, OTel or Vector metric aggregation, streaming aggregation in vmagent) drops pod or instance labels before remote write. Keep raw high-resolution data briefly locally if needed.

first_principles.problem: Per-pod series are needed only to compute per-service totals, yet all 3 million are stored long-term in the vendor.
truths: Raw data can be kept short-term.

analogy.title: Summarising receipts before filing
analogy.story: Keep daily totals per store in the archive; shred individual receipts after a week.
analogy.breaks: Shredded receipts can't be re-summed differently; choose aggregation labels carefully.

code.text:
groups:
  - name: service_aggregates
    rules:
      - record: service_route:http_requests:rate5m
        expr: sum by (service, route, status) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
# vmagent stream aggregation before remote write
# - match: 'http_requests_total'
#   interval: 1m
#   without: [pod, instance]
#   outputs: [total]

check.q: What do Prometheus recording rules do for cardinality and performance?
check.a: They pre-compute aggregated series on a schedule, so dashboards and long-term storage use far fewer, cheaper series.
